options.text: The clock starts when the organisation becomes aware of an incident likely to affect personal data.
The clock starts once the vendor can show that personal data was actually affected.
options.misconception: waits for proof of impact rather than for grounds to suspect

options.text: The clock starts when the regulator publishes the incident in its weekly bulletin.
options.misconception: waits for public disclosure before starting the clock

options.text: The clock starts when the post-incident review has been signed off internally.
options.misconception: starts the clock at the end of the internal paperwork

questions.explanation: The trigger is awareness of an incident likely to affect personal data, so waiting for proof or a public notice starts the clock too late. Investigation runs in parallel with the notification.
questions.hint: Awareness, not proof, starts the clock.

options.misconception: measures one failure instead of the requests met

questions.topic: How a contractual security requirement gets audited
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an audit of a contractual requirement tests
questions.stem: The survey notes record that a client's annexe is audited against a published framework. Write the explanation you would give.

answer.exemplar: The audit tests each contractual requirement by asking for the evidence that the requirement was actually operating, not by checking that a document exists, so a clause about privileged access review is satisfied by a set of dated review records with outcomes, and a clause about deletion is satisfied by configuration extracts showing the retention setting; where the evidence cannot be produced the clause is not met, whatever the policy promises.

questions.explanation: The explanation should show that the audit works on evidence of operation rather than on the existence of documents. That distinction is what a reader needs to see in the annexe.

options.text: Retest it and close it; the consequence is a cleaner register at the next review.
options.misconception: closes a finding on a single failed attempt

options.text: Retest it and keep it open; the consequence is a permanent warning on the system.
options.misconception: keeps an unreproducible finding as a permanent warning

options.text: Keep it open and escalate it; the consequence is work for the platform team with no result.
options.misconception: escalates instead of testing, producing work with no result

questions.explanation: A finding that cannot be reproduced is still a possibility, and only a repeat under the original conditions settles it. Retesting once and closing, or leaving it open forever, both dodge the decision.

questions.topic: Distinguishing an adversarial exercise from a vulnerability test

questions.stem: The relief layer shows two engagements. Write the note distinguishing an adversarial exercise from a vulnerability test.

answer.exemplar: A vulnerability test asks a bounded question about known weaknesses in named systems and produces findings that can be reproduced and ranked; an adversarial exercise asks what an attacker with a goal could achieve and produces a narrative of the path taken, including the points where the defenders noticed nothing; the first searches for faults and the second tests detection and decision, so their reports answer different questions and must not be counted in the same total.
